title: One deed tips the world (3:4)
hookLine: see yourself and the world as evenly balanced; your next deed could tip it
tomorrow: what is the shofar actually trying to say?

cards: Field day, tug-of-war. The rope has gone dead still, both sides straining, nobody moving. Then one kid at the very back digs in their heels, and the whole thing slides.

Can one small deed really tip the whole world? Maimonides says, in effect, yes, and the puzzle is how he gets there. He tells every person to see themselves as exactly half innocent and half guilty, all year long.
And the whole world, too: exactly half and half. Every person, every day, perfectly even? That can't be a headcount.

teach.b: It isn't. Read what comes next and the puzzle solves itself.

If a person does one wrong, he writes, they tip themselves and the whole world toward guilt, and bring ruin. If they do one mitzvah, one good deed, they tip themselves and the whole world toward merit, and bring rescue.
So the half-and-half isn't a report on anyone's record. It's a way of standing. Picture the scale perfectly level, and suddenly your next act isn't small.
It's the one that decides. A person who thinks they're mostly good can coast. A person who thinks they're mostly bad can give up.
Maimonides takes both excuses away with one picture: the scale is always even, and it's always your move.
He finds it in Proverbs: "the righteous is an everlasting foundation." He reads it as the one whose single good deed tipped the world and saved it.
The idea is older than him; the Talmud says something close, that a person should see themselves as half and half. Notice he isn't promising you'll see the result. Nobody gets to watch the scale.
You just act as if this deed is the one.

how: Some Jews take on an extra mitzvah or a little more tzedakah in the days around Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, drawing on Maimonides' picture of the evenly balanced scale.

games.q: what does “one deed tips the world” mean?
o: big public acts outweigh many small private ones
your next act could decide the balance of everything
the world is already doomed, whatever you do

p: how to see yourself, all year
tips you and the world toward guilt
tips you and the world toward merit
the righteous is an everlasting foundation

s: Maimonides claims the world's good and bad deeds are literally exactly even
it's a way of seeing yourself and the world, so your next deed counts as the decider.
Maimonides says one good deed can tip the whole world toward merit
one mitzvah tips you and the whole world, and brings rescue.
if you're mostly good already, one slip doesn't matter
the scale is always seen as level, so no deed is too small to decide it.

games.q: the group running Saturday's food drive says they have plenty of volunteers already. you were on the fence about going. what does 3:4 say?
o: go anyway; act as if your shift is the one that tips it.
stay home; they have enough, so one more person changes nothing.
go only if you can stay all day; a short shift barely counts.
games.why: Maimonides: see the scale as level, so your one deed is the decider. you don't get to see the result, only to act.

practice: Take a pen and a sticky note or scrap of paper. Write one small good deed you could do today, and when: a call, a dish washed, a thank-you sent.
Set it where you'll see it, then sit with the scale in your mind, perfectly level, waiting on you.

wordCard.voice: One deed tips the world: Maimonides' picture of a scale held perfectly even, so that your next act, good or bad, is the one that decides.

orig.note: Hebrew: the scale of merit, the side one good deed tips toward.

carryVoice: For the road: one deed tips the world, and the scale is level, waiting on your move. That's day fifteen forty-nine.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:4 (see yourself and the world as half and half; one deed tips the whole world)
Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 40b (a person should see themselves as half liable, half meritorious)
